item.title: TOP SHOTS (19 October 2026)
Executions of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia disappointing for us: Humaiun Kobir
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir has said the execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia following allegations of criminal offences is a matter of disappointment for Bangladesh.

He said there had been lapses in information-sharing and diplomatic communication over the recent executions of the two Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia. The government has sought a detailed explanation and information from the Saudi authorities regarding the incident, he added.

Humaiun Kobir made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday afternoon.

“Bangladesh has a good and deep relationship with Saudi Arabia, particularly at the level of our prime minister. Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both signatories to the Geneva Conventions. There was a gap in information-sharing in this incident. We have sought an explanation from Saudi Arabia to find out why this gap occurred. There was clearly a shortcoming somewhere in the information-sharing or the process. Both sides are holding discussions to look into the matter,” he said.

The state minister said, “This is certainly unfortunate. The execution was carried out following allegations or accusations of criminal offences, and that is disappointing for us. The sanctity of the House of Allah is sacred, and people travel to Mecca with pure intentions. If what we have heard and learned about this incident is true, it is naturally extremely unfortunate and in no way acceptable.”

Asked whether there was any possibility of compensation for the two Bangladeshis who had been executed, the state minister said, “No. The sentence has already been carried out. Once that happens, there is no longer any scope for that. We will now look into where the shortcomings occurred.”

Asked whether the identities of the two executed Bangladeshis had been confirmed, Humaiun Kobir said, “Both countries have signed the Geneva Conventions. If we apprehend a Saudi criminal here, we would certainly inform the Saudi authorities. That person would be entitled to consular services. In other words, they would at least be informed that their national had been involved in a criminal offence in Bangladesh.

“Likewise, we expect Saudi Arabia, or any other country, to inform us if one of our citizens is detained there. That is our expectation.”

Last Wednesday, several media outlets in Saudi Arabia and other parts of the Middle East reported that two Bangladeshis had been executed over allegations of committing an “immoral act” in the mosque area of the holy city of Mecca. Following the reports, Bangladesh’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs contacted the Saudi embassy in Dhaka.

On Sunday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs called Saudi Ambassador to Bangladesh Abdullah bin Zafer H Bin Abiyah to seek clarification regarding the executions of the two Bangladeshi nationals.

item.title: After son’s execution in Saudi Arabia, parents want to see his body just once
item.description:
Despite spending many years in Saudi Arabia, Abdul Bashir could not improve his family’s financial situation. After returning home in 2020, he took up farming. Hoping for a better life, he borrowed Tk 600,000 and sent his eldest son to Saudi Arabia in late 2022. But just eight months after arriving in the country, his son was arrested. At the time, Tk 450,000 of the loan remained unpaid.

Nearly three years after his son was arrested and imprisoned in Saudi Arabia, Bashir received devastating news last Wednesday, 14 October. He learned that his son had been executed. Since hearing the news, he has felt as though he is no longer truly alive, despite still breathing. Now, his only wish to have his son’s body brought back from Saudi Arabia so that he can see him one last time.

Bangladesh unaware of execution of 2 nationals in Mecca, writes to Saudi Arabia seeking details
Saudi Arabia executes two Bangladeshi for indecent acts inside Mecca mosque

Two Bangladeshi nationals were recently executed in Saudi Arabia after being convicted of committing an immoral act at a mosque in the holy city of Mecca. The Saudi Press Agency (SPA) confirmed the executions last Wednesday, citing the country’s Ministry of Interior. The two executed Bangladeshis were identified as Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhter.

Brahmanbaria Deputy Commissioner Md Abu Sayeed told Prothom Alo that they had learned about the matter and that the district administration would act in accordance with the government’s instructions.

Nazrul Islam, 25, was from a village in Brahmanbaria Sadar upazila. He was the eldest son of Abdul Bashir and Rahima Begum. Nazrul was the eldest of two brothers and two sisters. He passed the Dakhil examination from a madrasa in 2020 and subsequently enrolled in the humanities stream at a college in Sadar upazila.

2 Bangladeshis executed in Mecca, Govt seeks details from Saudi ambassador

Nazrul’s father had spent 24 years in Saudi Arabia before returning home in 2020. Despite his long years abroad, he had been unable to bring financial stability to the family. After returning, he began farming. Nazrul’s 14-year-old younger brother studies at a local Dakhil madrasa. One of his sisters, aged nine, is in Class Four at a government primary school, while the youngest is four.

Aunt dies after hearing the news

Family members said Nazrul went to Saudi Arabia in November 2022 and worked as a cleaner at the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca. Eight months after his arrival, Saudi police arrested him. He remained in prison from then on. The family learned of his arrest a month later.

Nazrul was occasionally allowed to speak to his parents over the phone for a few minutes. Their last conversation was on 11 October, when they spoke for about two to two and a half minutes. Then, at around 7:30pm Bangladesh time last Wednesday, someone called the family from Saudi Arabia and informed them that Nazrul had been executed.

Family members said Nazrul’s aunt, Abeda Begum, 65, fainted upon hearing the news of his execution. She died at around 2am that night.

Relatives and friends suspect a conspiracy

Nazrul’s relatives and friends remember him as a polite and well-mannered young man. They also claim that the allegations brought against him in Saudi Arabia are inconsistent with his character. They believe a conspiracy was behind the accusations.

Nazrul’s two distant cousins, Mostakim Bhuiyan and Imam Hasan Bhuiyan, told Prothom Alo that Nazrul had developed a dispute with someone while working as a cleaner in Saudi Arabia. He had told his uncle and aunt—his parents—about the matter over the phone. Nazrul had said that the person was a Pakistani national, they added.

They believe that person’s alleged conspiracy led to Nazrul’s fate.

Nazrul’s friend Rahat Bhuiyan said the allegations against him in Saudi Arabia were incompatible with his character. “I cannot believe that he would do something like this,” he said.

Maulana Naimur Rahman, superintendent of the local Dakhil madrasa where Nazrul studied, said Nazrul had been well-behaved and conducted himself properly.

“No one could say that the boy was ill-mannered or bad. I never saw anything in his behaviour while he was in Bangladesh that would suggest what is now being said about him,” he said.

Parents want to see their son’s body

The correspondent visited Nazrul’s home on Monday morning. As he spoke, his father, Abdul Bashir, repeatedly broke down in tears.

Bashir told Prothom Alo that he had borrowed Tk 600,000 from relatives to send his son to Saudi Arabia. During the first seven to eight months, Nazrul sent home around Tk 150,000. He had then spent three years in prison in Saudi Arabia.

“After hearing about my son’s death like this, my sister also suddenly died of a heart attack. Now, I am just waiting to see my son’s body,” he said.

Overcome with grief at the loss of her son, Rahima Begum has been crying continuously for the past several days.

“My son used to call once every month. We would speak for one or two minutes. The allegations against my son are false. I want to see my son’s body one last time,” she said.

item.title: Will Meta remain unaccountable for killings incited on Facebook?
item.description:
The first sentence under tech giant Meta’s ‘Violence and Incitement’ section states: “We aim to prevent potential offline violence that may be related to content on our platforms.”

Another line in the same section reads: “We remove language that incites or facilitates violence and credible threats to public or personal safety.”

All these conditions applied in the case of Wahiduzzaman Shamim of Debhata, Satkhira. Yet Shamim could not be saved. His killing was orchestrated through Facebook Live broadcasts on two occasions, along with several posts. The live videos were still available even two days after the incident. But Meta apparently still has not considered that such incitement on its Facebook platform could harm someone. Yet Shamim is dead.

People raised an outcry on Facebook itself over Shamim’s death, demanding justice. The person who incited the violence has also been arrested. Before long, images of another Shamim’s body will be circulating across Facebook. There is no need to revisit the administration’s inaction. But when such incidents repeatedly occur in this country as a result of calls for violence spread on Facebook, does the platform bear no responsibility? Should it not be held accountable?

One of the earliest widely discussed incidents of attacks incited through Facebook in Bangladesh took place 15 years ago, in 2012, in Ramu upazila of Cox’s Bazar. The Buddhist community faced a horrific attack. Such incitement has not stopped; rather, it has increased. The most extensive incident occurred in October 2021, when Facebook posts and videos surrounding allegations of desecration of the Holy Quran in Cumilla triggered communal violence in at least 18 districts of Bangladesh. According to Freedom House, at least 11 people were killed and hundreds injured in the violence. At the time, the government even suspended mobile internet services.

Meta continues to violate its own policies, people continue to die, yet the company faces no accountability. Given the behaviour of successive governments in Bangladesh, however, any digital-related policy introduced in the country is a cause for concern not only for citizens but also for these platforms. Before the most recent election, a policy introduced by the interim government effectively prompted Meta to threaten to suspend its services!

Over the past two years, incidents of attacks and killings incited through Facebook have been on the rise. Last December, evidence was found in 958 posts (according to a report jointly published by The Daily Star and DismissLab) of direct calls for attacks on Prothom Alo and The Daily Star or celebrations of such attacks. On the night of 18 December, Prothom Alo and The Daily Star came under attack, with their offices vandalised and set on fire. Udichi and Chhayanaut were also targeted. In April this year, a pir (priest) was killed in Daulatpur, Kushtia, following incitement on Facebook.

Meta’s own policies clearly prohibit incitement to violence, threats, harassment and the disclosure of personal information that could create a risk of physical harm. Its safety policies states they remove contents that include “violent speech targeting a person or group of people on the basis of their protected characteristic(s) or immigration status.” Meta “removes content, disables accounts and works with law enforcement when,” they “believe there is a genuine risk of physical harm or direct threats to public safety.”

They “also try to consider the language and context in order to distinguish casual or awareness-raising statements from content that constitutes a credible threat to public or personal safety. In determining whether a threat is credible, we may also consider additional information such as a person's public visibility and the risks to their physical safety.” Yet in Bangladesh, such contents have been allowed day after day!

Meta’s role came under scrutiny following the attacks on media outlets last December. The accounts of some influencers were shut down, although they have since opened new accounts on the same platform. In March this year, Amnesty International raised concerns about Meta’s role in Bangladesh. It warned that failure to take timely and effective action against harmful online content could increase the risk of real-world violence and serious human rights violations. It also referred to the threats and incitement circulated on Facebook ahead of the December attacks.

This raises the question: what measures are taken in developed countries when Meta violates its own policies? In January 2021, Facebook faced intense criticism following the violence at the US Capitol. Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg had to appear before the US Congress.

In 2024, Meta faced an investigation in the United Kingdom over its delayed response to the riots and the spread of incitement. Meanwhile, under the European Union’s Digital Services Act, social media platforms can be fined up to 6 per cent of their annual worldwide turnover if they fail to prevent the spread of violence or fake news.

The obvious question now is: has the Bangladesh government made any effort to hold these platforms accountable? It has made some efforts and continues to do so. However, while legislation in other countries is intended to prioritise the protection of citizens, in Bangladesh, it is aimed at ensuring the protection of ruling-party figures. As a result, whenever the question of holding giants such as Meta accountable comes to the fore, the issue of ‘restrictions on freedom of expression’ takes centre stage. During the previous Awami League government, such laws were grossly abused.

Recently, the government has taken steps to amend the Cyber Security Act. The proposed amendments include provisions for taking action against incitement to violence, hurting religious sentiments, cyber bullying, spreading false information and issuing threats. However, these provisions primarily concern actions to be taken by the government, not the platforms themselves.

For nearly four years, there have also been discussions about introducing a policy on social media and OTT platforms. During the Awami League government, there was a tussle between the telecommunications and information ministries over which ministry would be responsible for implementing the policy. The issue remained unresolved even under the interim government. Following the BNP's rise to power, there have been discussions about the Information Ministry drafting a law titled the ‘Social Media and Digital Intermediaries Act 2026’.

Meta continues to violate its own policies, people continue to die, yet the company faces no accountability. Given the behaviour of successive governments in Bangladesh, however, any digital-related policy introduced in the country is a cause for concern not only for citizens but also for these platforms. Before the most recent election, a policy introduced by the interim government effectively prompted Meta to threaten to suspend its services!

The interim government had included provisions for mandatory data localisation in Bangladesh and imprisonment for violations in its Personal Data Protection Ordinance, which angered Meta. Ruzan Sarwar, Meta’s Public Policy Manager for the Asia-Pacific region, expressed her displeasure at a conference organised by Digitally Right and EngageMedia last April.

On that occasion, she said Meta had considered suspending its services in Bangladesh because of the data localisation provision. However, the interim government dropped the provision shortly before its tenure ended. At the same conference in April, Ruzan Sarwar faced questions over the use of Meta to incite violence. However, she remarked that preventing offline violence is the responsibility of the government.

There has been criticism of Meta’s discriminatory treatment of countries in the Global South. In 2022, Amnesty International raised concerns about Meta’s discriminatory practices. In a report published at the time, it said Meta’s profit-driven algorithms and surveillance-based business models played a major role in amplifying ethnic discrimination, hate speech and violence in countries across the Global South.

An article published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance journal by Cambridge University Press in May 2025 stated that governments in the Global South have very little influence over social media policymaking. Citing religious tensions and attacks on minorities in Bangladesh, the article also criticised Meta’s “difficulties in identifying content in the Bangla language.”

Yet, is there no way to hold these platforms accountable? Instead of merely repeating the rhetoric of ‘open an office in this country’, can we not sit down and address the real challenges? Can we not find ways to seek redress?

Suhada Afrin is a journalist. The opinions expressed in this article are the author's own.

item.title: Admission policy for govt secondary schools: 55 students per section; fees, quota explained
item.description:
Government Secondary Schools across the country may admit students from Class One up to Class Nine, subject to the availability of vacant seats. Each section of a class may accommodate no more than 55 students. Children must be aged six or above to enter Class One.

The Ministry of Education has issued a new admission policy for government secondary schools across the country, incorporating these provisions.

All secondary schools must follow the policy for admissions for the 2027 academic year. The ministry published the policy on its website on Tuesday, 13 October 2026.

How old must students be?

In accordance with the “National Education Policy 2010”, schools must ensure that children are aged six or above when admitting them to Class One. However, on 1 January of the relevant academic year, a child's minimum age must be five and the maximum age seven.

Schools must calculate the ages of applicants to other classes according to the same criteria. Applicants must submit an attested copy of their online birth registration certificate with the admission application form to establish their age. Schools may allow children with special needs an additional age allowance of up to five years.

Academic year

Under the policy, the Secondary and Higher Education Division will determine the dates for online applications and the lottery for student admissions. The 2027 academic year will run from 1 January to 31 December. Each section of a class may admit no more than 55 students.

Rules for school preferences and admission tests

Admission to Class One will take place through a digital lottery. Schools must select all applicants for Class One through this lottery system.

Applicants for class one may rank a maximum of five institutions according to their preferences. However, if an applicant selects both shifts at a double-shift school, the system will count these choices as two school preferences.

If an applicant submits more than one application to the same institution, all of their applications will be cancelled.

The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) will centrally manage all aspects of the Class One admission process through a digital lottery. The authorities must conduct the lottery in the presence of admission committee members and ensure transparency throughout the process.

Alongside the list of students selected through the lottery, the authorities must prepare a waiting list containing as many applicants as there are vacant seats. If a selected student does not enroll by the deadline set by the admission committee, the school must offer admission to applicants from the waiting list in sequence.

The policy states that, before conducting the digital lottery, the authorities must have another government-recognised technical institution verify the reliability of the software developed by a technical institution selected by the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education. The authorities must retain the relevant certificate of verification.

Written examinations: Admission to classes two to nine

Schools must select students for vacant seats in classes two to nine according to merit based on written examinations.

Alongside the list of students selected through the written examinations, the authorities must prepare a waiting list containing as many applicants as there are vacant seats. If a selected student does not enrol by the deadline set by the admission committee, the school must offer admission to applicants from the waiting list in sequence.

Admission test marks distribution and duration

(a) Classes Two to Five: The admission test will carry a total of 50 marks, comprising 15 marks for Bangla, 15 for English and 20 for Mathematics. The examination will last one hour.

(b) Classes Six to Nine: The admission test will carry a total of 100 marks, comprising 30 marks for Bangla, 30 for English and 40 for Mathematics. The examination will last two hours.

In accordance with the admission committee’s decision, the head of each institution will publish an admission notice specifying the number of vacant seats. The admission committee will also ensure wide publicity by publishing notices in national and local newspapers, on websites and through other channels.

For admission to Class Six, schools will reserve 10 per cent of their total Class Six seats for students who have passed class five at independent government primary schools.

Grouping schools into clusters

For admission to class two to nine, the admission committee may divide schools into different clusters, taking into account their locations and the advantages and disadvantages for students. Each student may apply to one school of their choice within each cluster.

Application form fees and admission charges

The authorities may charge a maximum of Tk 110 for the online application form for admission to class one and Tk 250 for application forms for classes two to nine.

The authorities must determine admission fees, including session charges, in accordance with the Ministry of Education’s instructions.

Conducting the digital lottery and preparing results

After prospective students complete their online applications within the stipulated period, the technical institution responsible for conducting the digital lottery will provide the “Dhaka City Admission Committee” with all relevant application data and information required to publish the digital lottery results.

The authorities must conduct the Class One admission lottery under the supervision of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), in the presence of members of the “Dhaka City Admission Committee”.

Each educational institution will publish the list of selected students, obtained from the “Dhaka City Admission Committee”, on its website and display it on its noticeboard. Under no circumstances may an institution admit any student who does not appear on the list of selected candidates.

Preparing question papers

The admission committee will arrange for the preparation of question papers for admission tests for classes two to nine in due time. The questions must meet appropriate quality standards, suit the relevant class level and draw on the corresponding textbooks prescribed by the National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB).

The authorities must ensure confidentiality and security throughout the preparation and moderation of question papers.

Preparing results

The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education, the deputy commissioners’ offices and the schools’ websites, where available, will publish the merit lists and waiting lists simultaneously.

Headteachers will display the lists at their respective schools. The head of each educational institution must complete the admission process within the period set by the committee.

Without the admission committee’s approval, the head of an educational institution may not admit any student at their own discretion at any other time during the year. Any violation of this provision will be treated as a punishable offence.

The admission committee will preserve all documents relating to the admission tests, from the allocation of code numbers through to the preparation of results, for one year.

Reserved quotas, employee quota and admission for twins

*For admission to class six, schools will reserve 10 per cent of their total class six seats for students who have passed class five at independent government primary schools.

*Government schools in Dhaka metropolitan area must reserve 40 per cent of their seats for students living within their respective catchment areas. The remaining 60 per cent will remain open to all applicants. The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education will determine the catchment areas of all government schools in Dhaka metropolitan area and inform all relevant stakeholders.

*Schools will reserve five per cent of seats for the sons and daughters of freedom fighters and martyred freedom fighters. Applicants seeking admission under this quota must attach an attested copy of the relevant supporting documents to their applications and present the original documents at the time of admission. The authorities must verify the relevant freedom fighter certificate properly before completing the admission process. If no eligible applicants apply for these reserved seats, the authorities must allocate the first three per cent to applicants who are siblings of students and the remaining two per cent to general applicants, following the prescribed procedures. Under no circumstances may these seats remain vacant.

*To integrate students with special needs into mainstream education, schools will reserve two per cent of seats for them, provided they meet the minimum eligibility requirements. Applicants must submit certification from the appropriate authority as proof of eligibility. If no eligible applicants apply for these seats, the authorities must fill them with general applicants in accordance with the prescribed procedures. Under no circumstances may these seats remain vacant.

*A total of two per cent of seats at any government educational institution will be reserved for the children of officials and employees working at the Ministry of Education (one per cent) and those working at its subordinate offices and organisations listed in Schedule A (one per cent). Applicants must meet the minimum eligibility requirements and provide a certificate from the Secondary and Higher Education Division. Where the calculation produces a fraction, the authorities must round it up to the next whole number. If no eligible applicants apply for these seats, the authorities must fill them with general applicants in accordance with the prescribed procedures. Under no circumstances may these seats remain vacant.

*Schools will reserve three per cent of seats for applicants whose siblings are already enrolled at the institution, as well as for newly applying twins. However, this benefit will apply to a maximum of three children of any couple. If no applicants qualify under the sibling category at a particular institution, the three per cent allocation will be open to twins. If no eligible applicants apply for these seats, the authorities must fill them with general applicants in accordance with the prescribed procedures. Under no circumstances may these seats remain vacant.

*Schools will reserve a further two per cent of seats for applicants whose twin brothers or sisters are already enrolled at the institution, as well as for twins applying for admission together. However, this benefit will apply to a maximum of three children of any couple. If no twins apply for these seats at a particular institution, the two per cent allocation will be open to applicants whose siblings are already enrolled. If no eligible applicants apply for these seats, the authorities must fill them with general applicants in accordance with the prescribed procedures. Under no circumstances may these seats remain vacant.

item.title: I apologise if I made a mistake, but I did nothing wrong: Ishraque
item.description:
Ishraque Hossain has once again defended his actions during the controversial armed anti-narcotics operation, at a press conference called to announce his resignation as State Minister for Liberation War Affairs.

“If I made any mistake, or if I hurt anyone through this operation, I would first like to apologise for that. But I firmly believe that I did nothing wrong that day. I kept the firearm in my hand only for as long as necessary to protect myself. After that, it was no longer visible in my possession,” he said.

The press conference was held at the National Press Club in the capital on Monday afternoon. Ishraque arrived at the club’s Abdus Salam Hall with party activists at around 1.45 pm to attend the previously announced event.

His supporters chanted various slogans in his name. The press conference began at around 2:00 pm.

Speaking about his resignation, Ishraque said, “As of today, I have voluntarily sought release from my responsibilities as State Minister for the Ministry of Liberation War Affairs from the honourable Prime Minister. I told him that I wanted to work throughout this period to eliminate drugs in Dhaka-6, the adjoining areas and any other areas that might subsequently be assigned to me, as well as to address other problems affecting our national public life. He kindly agreed and gave me the opportunity, saying, ‘All right, go and identify the area and work there.’”

Ishraque Hossain added that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had included him in his first Cabinet following the election. He said he had been serving as state minister in what he described as one of the country’s most prestigious ministries, responsible for Liberation War Affairs.

Ishraque said he subsequently met the prime minister and briefed him on the severity of the drug problem. During the meeting, he told the prime minister that he wanted to resign, explaining that he did not want his actions to overshadow the prime minister’s work.

“I have come here today to address an important issue that has generated considerable discussion over the past two or three days. Various reports have appeared in domestic and international media. Some have been factual, while others have been exaggerated to varying degrees. I am here today primarily to explain in detail what actually happened that day,” he said.

Ishraque said he had visited Ghuntighar according to a pre-arranged plan and had informed the local police station before going there. He said he routinely carried his licensed firearm at his waist and had taken it in his hand so that he could protect himself if a threatening situation arose.

He added that the viral video had helped establish that the drug users did not have firearms in their possession.

Ishraque said he had visited a Durga Puja mandap after the incident. Later that night, he noticed that a video of the operation had gone viral and that media outlets were publishing reports under various headlines.

He noted that the prime minister had visited 13 locations across the capital that day, describing those visits as commendable. However, he claimed that the way the media had covered his own incident had overshadowed the prime minister’s activities.

Ishraque HossainIf I made any mistake, or if I hurt anyone through this operation, I would first like to apologise for that. But I firmly believe that I did nothing wrong that day.

Ishraque said he subsequently met the prime minister and briefed him on the severity of the drug problem. During the meeting, he told the prime minister that he wanted to resign, explaining that he did not want his actions to overshadow the prime minister’s work.

He nevertheless announced that his campaign against drugs would continue.

On Sunday, several senior sources close to the government said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had instructed Ishraque Hossain to resign from the Cabinet.

According to the sources, the prime minister summoned Ishraque after a Cabinet meeting at the Secretariat on Sunday afternoon and directed him to step down.

Ishraque Hossain steps down from cabinet

On Saturday, Ishraque had taken part in an anti-narcotics operation in Ghuntighar, Gandaria, in the capital, raising a firearm. Others accompanying him were also carrying weapons. After footage of the incident circulated on social media, questions were raised about a state minister participating in an operation while openly displaying a firearm.

The incident caused unease and discontent within both the ruling BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) and the government. Government and party figures considered the episode particularly embarrassing as Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was conducting surprise visits to hospitals, educational institutions and government residential areas across the capital to assess conditions.

Facing criticism, Ishraque issued a statement on his verified Facebook page claiming that he had visited the area to participate in a social resistance initiative against drugs.

He said the programme had been organised through a joint decision involving police, local political leaders and community leaders.

Ishraque loses ministerial position due to showy display of power

At around 10:00 pm on Sunday, Prothom Alo published a report headlined “Prime Minister orders Ishraque to resign from Cabinet”. Following its publication, Ishraque issued a series of Facebook posts and WhatsApp audio messages describing the report as a rumour. His press officer also issued a rebuttal, calling the report “false and misleading”.

However, shortly after 8.30 am on Monday, Ishraque himself announced his resignation on Facebook. He subsequently made the announcement formally at the National Press Club press conference in the afternoon.

item.title: Lalon's humanist philosophy draws thousands to annual shrine gathering
item.description:
Thousands of devotees, mystics and visitors gathered at the shrine of Fakir Lalon Shah in Chheuriya, Kushtia, to mark the 136th death anniversary of the Baul mystic, philosopher and poet, celebrating his humanist philosophy through spiritual rituals, mystic songs and discussions.

The three-day programme, which began on Saturday, will conclude late Monday with cultural events and a rural fair on the shrine premises.

The main spiritual gathering, known as Sadhusanga, ended on Sunday after that devotees completed the principal rituals.

The morning ritual, Balyaseba, was held on Sunday, followed by Purna Seba at noon, formally concluding the Sadhusanga. Most devotees began leaving the shrine in the afternoon, while others planned to stay until Monday to complete their spiritual obligations.

Time bomb recovered from Lalon’s shrine in Kushtia, BGB deployed

For many, the annual gathering is an opportunity to reconnect with spiritual guides, practise mystic traditions and reflect on Lalon Shah's teachings on humanity, equality, self-purification and communal harmony.

Nizam Fakir, who travelled from Gaibandha, said he visits the shrine every year to take part in Sadhusanga, where mystics and spiritual guides from different parts of the country gather.

He said the formal rituals included Adhibas, Rakhal Seba, Balyaseba and Purna Seba.

Mamun Sadhu said devotees felt like members of one family when they gathered at the shrine.

Through Sadhusanga, they could spend time with spiritual guides and practise Lalon Shah's humanist philosophy and mystic traditions, he said, adding that the completion of Purna Seba marked the time for farewells.

A female student of the University of Chittagong said she had come to learn about Lalon Shah's philosophy, particularly his opposition to social discrimination.

She hoped to return with a deeper understanding of his messages of humanity, equality and positive thinking.

The rural fair, running alongside the spiritual programme, continued to attract visitors on Monday, even as many devotees departed after completing the rituals.

The anniversary programme was held from 17 to 19 October at Lalon Shah's shrine in Chheuriya Akhra Bari, under Kumarkhali upazila of Kushtia district, drawing thousands of followers and visitors from home and abroad.

The district administration and law enforcement agencies put in place a multi-layered security arrangement to ensure the event proceeded peacefully and in an orderly manner.

Deputy Commissioner Touhid Bin Hasan told BSS that the anniversary was more than a commemorative occasion, offering an opportunity to promote Lalon Shah's humanist philosophy, secular outlook and message of communal harmony.

He said the administration had taken necessary measures to ensure visitors' safety and maintain law and order, with law enforcement agencies and relevant departments working together throughout the festival.

Lalon Shah died on the first day of Kartik in 1297 Bangla year. Since then, his followers have observed his death anniversary through commemorative programmes, which later expanded with initiatives from Lalon Academy and the district administration.

Over the years, the annual gathering has become a major cultural and spiritual event, bringing together people from diverse backgrounds to engage with the mystic poet's songs and enduring message of love, humanity and equality.

item.title: The structural trap: How banking arbitrage starves our capital market
item.description:
Whenever discussions turn to Bangladesh’s perpetually underdeveloped capital market, observers point to poor corporate governance and lax regulatory enforcement. Governance in our financial sector is undeniably weak, and elevating it is urgent. Yet, treating governance failure in isolation misdiagnoses the problem. Governance standards do not materialise out of thin air; they reflect the incentives embedded within the financial architecture. Without decisive structural reform, appropriate governance cannot be achieved or sustained.

The root bottleneck holding back our bond and equity markets is structural: our financial ecosystem makes commercial bank credit artificially cheap and opaque. Commercial banks often operate on paper-thin real capital. Regulators allow them to fund multi-year industrial assets using short-term, low-cost deposits. This creates an overwhelming incentive for corporate borrowers to shun public markets. Consequently, long-term industrial risks sit concentrated inside the banking sector, generating recurring cycles of unpaid loans and acute liquidity crunches.

The asymmetry: Why issuers avoid public markets

In a balanced economy, fixed capital investments like factories and infrastructure rely on long-term debt or equity backed by institutional investors. In Bangladesh, corporate borrowers bypass public markets in favor of bilateral bank loans due to deep structural asymmetries.
Issuing a corporate bond requires audited records, credit rating surveillance, detailed prospectuses, and continuous public accountability.

Bilateral bank credit, by contrast, is negotiated privately with flexible covenants and minimal disclosure. Furthermore, commercial banks have historically extended long-term project loans without pricing in term or liquidity risks. They rely on cheap retail deposits, policy refinance lines, and implicit expectations of regulatory forbearance. Corporates also rarely commit to rigid bond repayment schedules. Instead, they fund long-gestation assets by rolling over short-term working capital facilities indefinitely, converting short-term facilities into de facto perpetual debt with zero market discipline.

The capital illusion: Profitability over solvency

A central driver of this fragile dynamic is how banks are evaluated by regulators, boards, and the market. Public discourse routinely celebrates accounting profitability and balance-sheet expansion while ignoring underlying capital metrics.

Banks frequently report robust operating profits and announce dividends based on accrued interest income from rescheduled and repeatedly rolled-over loans—cash flows that have never actually entered their vaults. Thinly capitalised banks carry immense duration and credit risks without setting aside realistic risk-weighted capital buffers under Basel III.

Evaluating a bank primarily on loan growth and paper profits rather than real Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital creates a severe moral hazard. It encourages lenders to extend high-risk, long-term credit on fragile equity to maximise short-term accounting returns. At the same time, it conceals true solvency problems until a macroeconomic shock forces a sudden, costly recognition of bad assets. A financial system where banks project paper health on eroded capital bases destroys any incentive for long-term risks to migrate to the capital market.

Synthetic project finance: Arbitrage beyond borders

This structural distortion extends beyond domestic currency loans into cross-border credit. During the era of near-zero global interest rates and a tightly managed currency peg, banks and corporates turned routine trade tools, such as Usance Payable at Sight (UPAS) deferred letters of credit, into synthetic project finance.

While elevating governance standards across both banks and corporates is non-negotiable, governance will not thrive in a fundamentally broken market structure

Borrowers used these low-interest, short-term foreign currency facilities to import capital machinery for non-export projects that earned revenue exclusively in BDT. When global interest rates climbed and the currency depreciated, the cost of servicing this unhedged foreign debt surged by 30 to 40 percent. Importers could not settle these ballooning foreign obligations. Banks then converted unpaid liabilities into overdue local currency loans on their own balance sheets, evolving from an easy regulatory arbitrage into a systemic shock that strained national reserves and drained interbank liquidity.

Why governance requires structural counterparties

The traditional response to financial distress has been purely administrative. The central bank issues circulars capping lending rates, ordering restructuring mandates, and offering forbearance packages. While governance standards are lacking and must be upgraded, administrative circulars alone cannot manufacture good governance.

Governance is an equilibrium outcome of stakeholder consensus. In an ecosystem dominated by a tight nexus of large borrowers and closely held banks, incentives naturally align around continuous loan rollovers and regulatory forbearance. Without independent market counterparties who possess an economic stake in transparency, administrative mandates merely push risk into creative accounting maneuvers. Robust governance takes root only when borrowers answer to diverse capital market participants, such as pension trustees, institutional bondholders, and independent asset managers, who possess both the legal standing and the financial incentive to enforce debt covenants.

Fixing the financial ecosystem

To break this structural trap, policymakers must align banking regulations with capital market development.

Regulators must enforce strict capital realism by mandating significantly higher risk-weighted capital charges on long-duration corporate exposures held on bank balance sheets. Authorities should end the practice of treating accounting profit as a proxy for financial health, enforcing verified CET1 capital adequacy before allowing dividend payouts or balance-sheet expansion.

Simultaneously, policy must eliminate synthetic long-term bank credit by enforcing strict single-borrower caps and prohibiting repeated rollovers of short-term credit for capital equipment. To build market depth, authorities need to establish clear statutory mandates for provident funds and insurance companies to deploy a designated portion of their assets into rated corporate bonds. Developing a liquid secondary market for government securities across various maturities will then provide the transparent, risk-free benchmark yield curve necessary to price private corporate debt accurately.

Moving forward

Bangladesh cannot fund multi-decade industrialisation on the back of 3-month retail deposits and thinly capitalised banks. While elevating governance standards across both banks and corporates is non-negotiable, governance will not thrive in a fundamentally broken market structure.

Until policy restores capital discipline to commercial banking and dismantles the structural arbitrage that makes long-term bank lending deceptively cheap, governance will remain a hollow buzzword, capital markets will remain sidelined, and the banking sector will remain the epicenter of macroeconomic vulnerability.

* Sajed ul Islam is a senior banking executive and financial markets specialist with three decades of global institutional experience across treasury, capital markets, and corporate governance.

item.title: Kobir: Execution of two Bangladeshis in KSA very disappointing
item.description:
Describing the execution of two Bangladeshis as “very disappointing”, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Monday said Bangladesh has sought an explanation from its friendly country, Saudi Arabia, over it, citing a possible gap in information sharing and communication between the two countries.
“We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions,” he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The state minister, however, said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his government enjoyed good and deep relations with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, expressing hope that the ties would reach a new height.
He said there appeared to have been a lapse somewhere in the process.
Talking to reporters separately, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said they are still waiting for a copy of the verdict to know in detail.
“Please wait until we receive a copy of the verdict (from the Saudi authorities),” she said.
Bangladesh on Sunday sought further information from Saudi Arabia regarding the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals, raising the issue with Saudi Ambassador to Bangladesh Dr Abdullah Zafer bin Abiyah.
Secretary (East & West) Dr Md Nazrul Islam sought detailed information about the executions during a meeting with the Saudi Ambassador, a senior official at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs told UNB.
When asked whether the move could be described as summoned, another official told UNB, “No, it was not.”
Although Dhaka raised the issue with the Saudi envoy, it expressed confidence that the incident would not affect the strong bilateral relations between the two countries.
The importance of staying “mindful” of the laws of the host country was also discussed.
Both sides expressed satisfaction with the steady progress of cooperation between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia across various sectors.
On Saturday, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said the government had yet to receive detailed official information from Saudi authorities regarding the execution of a Bangladeshi man and a woman, adding that such unfortunate news was unexpected.
“We have yet to receive any official detailed information from the Saudi government,” she told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, noting that Bangladesh sent a letter to the Saudi government requesting detailed information.
Earlier, Saudi media reported that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia executed the two Bangladeshis after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque in the holy city of Mecca.
Quoting the Saudi Interior Ministry, Gulf News reported that the court imposed the sentences because of the seriousness of the offence, the violation of the sanctity of the mosque, and the circumstances in which the acts were committed.
The Saudi authorities identified the two Bangladeshis as Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Siti Akhtar.
“On October 14, we learned that two Bangladeshi nationals had been sentenced to death under Saudi Arabian law and that the executions had been carried out,” the State Minister said, noting that neither the Ministry of Foreign Affairs nor the Bangladesh Mission in Saudi Arabia had been informed in advance.
“We wanted to know whatever we needed to know. Let the reply come. I will be able to let you know,” Shama said.
Upon learning of the incident, the Bangladesh Mission notified the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, sharing all the information it had gathered from Saudi authorities.
The state minister said the government sent a formal inquiry to ascertain the full details, including the identities of the individuals, their backgrounds in Bangladesh, and when they had originally arrived in Saudi Arabia for work.
Based on past experience, the state minister said Saudi Arabia has its own legal framework and that anyone found guilty of a grave offence is punished in accordance with the country’s laws.
“The execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia serves as a major lesson for us,” she said.
Shama Obaid said the repatriation of the bodies could be arranged once a response to the letter is received from Saudi Arabia.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,201 as five more die in 24 hours
item.description:
Five more children died with measles-like symptoms across the country in the past 24 hours, although no deaths from confirmed measles were reported during the period.
The deaths occurred between 8:00am on Sunday and 8:00am on Monday, according to a press release issued by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
The DGHS said 1,097 children have died with measles-like symptoms since March 15, while 104 died after being diagnosed with measles. The combined death toll from measles and measles-like symptoms has now reached 1,201.
In the past 24 hours, 1,307 suspected measles cases and 35 confirmed cases were reported nationwide.
Since March 15, a total of 190,663 suspected measles patients have been admitted to hospitals, with 183,042 recovering and being discharged.
According to the DGHS, 214,551 people have developed measles-like symptoms since March 15, while 23,157 cases of measles have been confirmed during the period.

item.title: Rioting cases fall 72.6% in Jan-Sept 2026
item.description:
Reported rioting incidents in Bangladesh fell by 72.6% in January-September 2026 compared to the corresponding period of 2025, marking the steepest percentage decline among the four crime categories covered by the nine-month comparison, according to data from the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The number of reported rioting incidents dropped to 17 from 62, a reduction of 45 cases. The data also showed declines in reported violence against women, child abuse and kidnapping during the same period.
Reported violence against women fell from 9,262 cases in January-September 2025 to 8,178 in the corresponding period of 2026, a decrease of 1,084 cases, or 11.7%.
Child abuse cases declined from 3,591 to 3,151, down by 440 cases, or 12.3%.
Kidnapping incidents also decreased, falling from 812 to 769, a reduction of 43 cases, or 5.3%.
Among these four categories, violence against women recorded the largest numerical reduction, while rioting registered the largest percentage decline.
Separate figures for July-September also showed declines across all seven crime categories included in the comparison: rioting, theft, child abuse, kidnapping, robbery, dacoity and murder.
Rioting incidents fell from nine in July-September 2025 to five in the same period of 2026, a decrease of four cases, or 44.4%.
Robbery recorded the second-largest percentage decline in the quarterly comparison, falling from 171 cases to 123, down by 48 cases, or 28.1%.
Kidnapping incidents decreased from 295 to 242, a reduction of 53 cases, or 18%. Child abuse cases fell from 1,432 to 1,238, down by 194 cases, or 13.5%.
Murder cases declined from 980 to 881, a decrease of 99 cases, or 10.1%. Dacoity incidents fell from 511 to 467, down by 44 cases, or 8.6%.
Theft recorded the smallest percentage decline among the seven categories, falling from 2,693 cases in July-September 2025 to 2,576 in the corresponding period of 2026, a reduction of 117 cases, or 4.3%.

item.title: PM urges officials to keep Dhaka clean for their own children
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday urged city corporation officials and employees to work sincerely to make the capital clean, healthy and liveable, at least for the sake of their own children, saying waste and poor sanitation are among Dhaka’s biggest problems.
“Forget about everyone else. Let us build a healthy environment and a healthy city for our own children. Let us all work together towards that goal,” he said.
The prime minister made the call while exchanging views with officials and employees during a visit to Dhaka South City Corporation’s (DSCC) Nagar Bhaban headquarters, said the PM’s Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu.
Emphasizing the need to keep the city clean for the sake of children's future, Tarique said no parent would want their children to grow up in a dirty, germ-ridden and unhealthy environment.
Children do not stay only around their homes; they also go to schools, colleges, playgrounds and other parts of the city, he said, adding that efforts to keep Dhaka clean must extend beyond individual neighborhoods.
“Your children will not stay only in your neighborhood. They will move around the whole of Dhaka. So, let us all try together. If we make an effort, we can do it,” Tarique said.
About waste and poor cleanliness issues in the capital, he said the problems could not be solved in a day or even in seven days, but sincere and sustained efforts by everyone could gradually improve the situation.
Addressing city corporation officials and employees, the prime minister said they are directly or indirectly involved in resolving the problem.
“It may take time, but if you keep trying, change will come. You must have that confidence. The most important thing is the willingness to act,” he said.
Tarique also urged officials to take greater responsibility for identifying and resolving problems, saying he regularly looked for problems wherever he went and contacted the relevant people to address them.
“If you also observe problems in this way and take steps to solve them, change is certainly possible,” he said.
Citing London as an example, the prime minister said many parts of the British capital were also littered during the 1960s and 1970s. Still, sustained efforts and public awareness gradually improved the situation.
Many people who visited clean and well-maintained cities abroad might have wished Dhaka could be like them, he said, adding that regret alone would not bring change unless people also fulfilled their responsibilities.
Referring to a recent conversation with a senior official of a South Korean company that has been doing business in Bangladesh for a long time, Tarique said the official told him that Dhaka’s cleanliness improved somewhat compared with the past.
“He did not say there has been a big change. He said it has improved somewhat. That means change is possible. If we all work together, we can do even better,” the Prime Minister said.
He also said he regularly monitor the condition of roads and waste management across the city.
Some road dividers are being rebuilt, while condition at some waste transfer stations has improved to a certain extent, he said, stressing the need to continue such initiatives.
Tarique urged officials and employees to practice self-criticism alongside criticism of others.
“You may criticize me, but you must also examine yourselves. Think about how properly you are performing your duties and how much effort you are making,” he said.
Earlier, the prime minister visited the emergency operations centre at Nagar Bhaban, where he reviewed websites displaying weather information, earthquake updates from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), wind speed, flood forecasts and air quality.
He also enquired about how the information was monitored and how officials tracked emergency situations.
Tarique monitored the city's cleanliness activities through a Facebook Live broadcast and watched a video on the development and various activities of Dhaka South City Corporation.
State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam, DSCC Administrator Abdus Salam, Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan Milton, and Local Government Division Senior Secretary Shahidul Hasan were present.

item.title: Govt trains aspiring entrepreneurs to improve agro-processing skills
item.description:
The government is providing training to help young people become entrepreneurs by improving their agricultural product processing, business management skills and market access.
The initiative is being implemented in 208 upazilas across all 64 districts under a project of the Department of Agricultural Marketing (DAM) under the Ministry of Agriculture. So far, 6,875 people have received training, while the project aims to train around 7,000 more entrepreneurs this year.
The initiative is being implemented under the Programme on Agricultural and Rural Transformation for Nutrition, Entrepreneurship and Resilience in Bangladesh (PARTNER). Its objectives include creating entrepreneurs in various agriculture-based sectors, adding value to agricultural products, and expanding opportunities for processing and exports.
The project aims to ensure that women account for 60% of the entrepreneurs developed under the initiative, while men will make up the remaining 40%.
Project officials said training is being provided to develop entrepreneurs in various sectors, including agriculture, seeds, nurseries, mushrooms, vermicompost, jute products and dairy products. Alongside technical training, the initiative focuses on strengthening business skills, management knowledge and market linkages.
Dr Muhammad Abdullah Al Faruk, agency program director of the PARTNER-DAM component of the Department of Agricultural Marketing, said the initiative was underway in 208 upazilas across all 64 districts.
He said the training was designed to improve entrepreneurs' business management skills and connect them with markets.
After completing the training, entrepreneurs are also receiving incubation support, he said. Incubation support organisations are working to identify the challenges entrepreneurs face in running their businesses and help them find solutions.
The project also plans to provide financial assistance to trained entrepreneurs to purchase agricultural product processing equipment. Under the proposed arrangement, the project will subsidise 70% of the equipment costs, while entrepreneurs will bear the remaining 30%.
The support is expected to create opportunities for small entrepreneurs to launch and expand agricultural product processing businesses.
Another key objective of the project is to improve coordination among stakeholders involved in agricultural marketing. To this end, 767 Market Actors Business Schools have been established in different agricultural production areas under the Department of Agricultural Marketing. Of these, 227 focus on potatoes. The project plans to establish another 335 schools this year.
Dr Al Faruk said the schools were being established around the dominant agricultural products of particular areas.
The initiative brings farmers, traders, entrepreneurs, cold storage owners, transport operators and other market stakeholders under a common platform. This is expected to make it easier to identify challenges and opportunities in the supply chains of specific agricultural products, he said.
The project is also working to improve the value chains of potatoes, mangoes, jackfruits, tomatoes and aromatic rice.
It aims to strengthen coordination among stakeholders at different stages, from production and collection to storage, processing and marketing. Initiatives are also underway to form Value Chain Promotional Bodies for the five products.
Project officials said the guidelines for these bodies had already been approved by the ministry.
Meanwhile, Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid has stressed the importance of research, innovation and modern technology in increasing productivity across agriculture-based sectors.
He said research, innovation and the development of a skilled workforce were essential to advancing the agriculture, fisheries and livestock sectors. The government aims to develop skilled human resources in agriculture through training, he added.
Abul Kalam Azad, the project's coordinator, said entrepreneurs could create employment opportunities for others while becoming self-reliant themselves.
Initiatives to develop entrepreneurs could play an important role in making agriculture a modern and respected profession, he added.

item.title: UN agency slashes Gaza food aid over funding, warns needs persist
item.description:
The World Food Program said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, despite acute needs in the war-battered Palestinian territory.
With the cutbacks, 1.1 million Palestinians in Gaza -- still about half the population -- will be receiving either food or cash assistance each month from the UN agency, in reduced amounts.
The World Food Program said its efforts had mitigated the effects during a famine last year in Gaza -- a description of the situation disputed by Israel -- and warned that conditions had not improved to the point that it can take away aid.
“People are not safe. Airstrikes continue on a daily basis. People continue to be displaced,” Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told AFP at the agency’s office in east Jerusalem.
“Almost everybody remains without a permanent home to live in. And the humanitarian conditions are brutal,” he said.
According to the latest assessments, 1.4 million people -- or two-thirds of Gaza’s population -- are still “acutely food insecure” and need humanitarian assistance to survive, he said.
In August last year, the UN’s Integrated Food Security Phase Classification said that Gaza was suffering famine conditions. Israel, which has blockaded the territory and attacked it relentlessly since the October 7, 2023 resistance campaign on it by Hamas, described the finding as a lie.
The famine classification was lifted in December, two months after a US-brokered ceasefire was announced in Gaza. Israel has kept striking Gaza since then, vowing to kill anyone involved in the October 7 resistance campaign.
Since the ceasefire, the WFP has been able to step up assistance and had been reaching between 1.5 million and 1.8 million people every month.
“This has been a lifeline. But now, rather than being able to sustain and scale up that assistance, we’re actually having to reduce it,” Hughes said.
“And that’s not because we don’t have humanitarian access to deliver food; that’s because we don’t have funding.”
In addition to reducing the number of people who receive rations, the WFP has been forced to shrink the content.
Families receiving food assistance will now get only one food parcel instead of two and a smaller bag of wheat flour, the WFP said in an operational note.
The 75,000 families who receive assistance in cash will see the amount reduced from 1,250 to 750 shekels ($400 to $240) per month.
The WFP is funded by governments as well as private donors. It has seen a sharp drop in resources, including after President Donald Trump returned to power in the United States and drastically slashed contributions to UN agencies as well as bilateral aid.
The agency says it needs about $450 million over the next six months for its operations in Gaza and the West Bank, but in 2026 it has only received about half the usual financing for the Palestinian territories.
In September, the agency also reduced by half the number of aid recipients in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, from 400,000 to 200,000.
“Now is not the time in the history of Palestine and Gaza to turn away from what is happening in Gaza,” Hughes said.
The WFP says that conditions have moderately improved in Gaza but noted that needs could rise again with the onset of winter.
Israel has allowed more goods into Gaza under the terms of the Trump ceasefire but still imposes heavy restrictions, turning away shipments of anything that is seen as having potential military use -- a policy that has included blocking even prosthetic limbs, according to the United Nations.
Israel has ramped up longstanding criticism of the United Nations since the Gaza war, accusing the world body of bias and perpetuating dependency among Palestinians.

item.title: Maha Ashtami celebrated with Kumari Puja, Sandhi Puja
item.description:
Maha Ashtami, the third day of the six-day Sharadiya Durga Puja festival, is being celebrated across the country on Monday with due religious fervour and festivity.
Maha Ashtami Kalparambha and Bihit Puja were held this morning at temples across the country, including Dhakeshwari National Temple. Devotees later offered anjali (prayers) and received charanamrito (sacred water). Maha Prasad was also distributed among devotees.
Sandhi Puja was held from 7:55am to 8:43am, marking the transitional moment between Ashtami and Navami.
According to Hindu mythology, the ritual commemorates the moment when Goddess Durga assumed the form of Chamunda to slay the demon brothers Chanda and Munda.
Kumari Puja, a traditional ritual in which a young, unmarried girl is worshipped as an embodiment of Goddess Durga and the divine feminine, was held at some temples across the country.
In the capital, Kumari Puja was held at Ramakrishna Math and Ramakrishna Mission Dhaka at 9:30am.
During the ritual, an unmarried pre-pubescent girl, generally aged between one and 16, is worshipped as the living embodiment of the divine feminine and Goddess Durga.
Devotees offer water, clothes, flowers, and gold and silver ornaments at the feet of the Kumari as part of the special ritual.
Puja mandaps across the country have been bustling with devotees and visitors since last Friday, when the six-day festival began with the ceremonial invocation of Goddess Durga on Maha Shashthi.
Vibrant decorations, traditional dhak beats, the ringing of kashor and ghonta, conch-shell blasts and ululation have added to the festive atmosphere.
Devotees have been visiting puja pandals across the country to offer prayers and enjoy the celebrations.
A total of 33,851 puja mandaps have been set up across the country this year, including 258 in the capital, according to the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad. The number has increased by nearly 1,500 compared to last year.
The Gulshan-Banani Puja Foundation is hosting one of the most elaborate celebrations at Kamal Ataturk Park in Banani. Makeshift pandals at Kalabagan ground and Khamarbari have also emerged as major attractions for visitors in the capital, with large structures and eye-catching lighting displays drawing crowds.
Maha Navami will be celebrated tomorrow with religious fervour and enthusiasm. Devotees will gather at temples and mandaps to offer anjali, while major concluding worship rituals and the offering of bhog will mark the day.
Bijaya Dashami will be celebrated on Wednesday, marking the farewell to Goddess Durga. Devotees will take the idols in processions to designated rivers, ponds and other water bodies for immersion, known as Bisarjan.
In the capital, a large number of Durga Puja celebrations are being held in the old parts of the city, including Tantibazar and Shakharibazar.
Ramna Kali Mandir, Siddheshwari Kali Mandir, Dhaka University's Jagannath Hall and Uttara Sarbajanin Mandir are also witnessing large numbers of visitors every day during the festival.

item.title: Record El Nino? Depends who’s counting
item.description:
Britain’s Met Office says this year’s El Nino is “unprecedented.” Japan’s weather agency has called it the strongest ever observed. US forecasters say it still trails the biggest events in its record books.
How can they all be right?
The answer lies in how they measure El Nino’s strength, with meteorological agencies using different methods to assess the climate phenomenon that make direct comparisons difficult.
“By any measure, we are looking at a very strong El Nino,” climate scientist Emily Becker of the University of Miami told AFP, adding that only once it is over will scientists be able to assess how big it is and “where it fits in the context of history.”
The Pacific Ocean’s El Nino Southern Oscillation (Enso) is the planet’s main natural climate driver. Normally, trade winds blow east to west along the equator, pushing warm water from South America toward Asia, while cold water rises from the depths to replace it.
El Ninos, which occur every two to seven years on average and last nine to 12 months, disrupt this pattern.
The trade winds weaken and warm water is pushed back east toward the Americas. That shift in where ocean heat is released into the atmosphere ripples across global weather, making some regions cooler and wetter and others hotter and drier.
In describing the El Nino as unprecedented, the Met Office points to raw temperatures in the Pacific.
“Our observations confirm that sea-surface temperatures in the central equatorial Pacific have now surpassed levels recorded during previous El Nino events,” it said in a statement to AFP.
But absolute temperatures are just one way of measuring El Nino’s strength. Agencies also look at anomalies -- how far temperatures rise above a historic baseline -- to assess the event.
The Japan Meteorological Agency last week declared this El Nino the strongest on record based on how far sea surface temperatures were above normal in the Nino3 region of the eastern Pacific. By its count, the event beat 1997 in observations going back to 1949.
The US watches a neighboring box, Nino3.4, in the east-central Pacific.
It declares an El Nino when temperatures there run at least 0.5C above normal and the atmosphere responds, weakening the trade winds and shifting tropical rainfall eastward. This process is known as “ocean-atmosphere coupling.”
How “normal” is defined has been a matter of significant debate.
The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) and other agencies including the UN’s World Meteorological Organization long used the Oceanic Nino Index (ONI), which compares temperatures to a 30-year average that is updated every five years, so that the baseline keeps pace with a warming climate.
But with climate change speeding up and warming oceans worldwide, Noaa now uses the Relative Oceanic Nino Index (Roni), and the WMO is in the process of switching.
RONI also relies on a 30-year average but goes on to measure how warm or cool the east-central Pacific is compared to the rest of the tropical ocean, because it is that difference that drives the weather impacts we care about.
“We were finding a mismatch between the temperature of the tropical Pacific and the impacts,” said Becker about the old index. La Nina years, when the central and eastern tropical Pacific is cooler than normal, were producing stronger effects than their rating suggested, and El Ninos weaker ones.
Noaa projects this El Nino will be the strongest in its records, which go back to 1950, if the three-month average Roni anomaly reaches 2.5°C or higher, a level that would put it above the 1982-83, 2015-16, and 1997-98 events.
The chances are rated “high,” but not yet certain.
“Regardless of where we’re ranking or how we’re measuring this event, it’s an incredible opportunity to study and understand this very powerful phenomenon in the context of a warming world,” said Becker.
